title: Microsoft Agent Framework Harness and Hosted Agents Reach General Availability
gist: Microsoft's Agent Framework has crossed from SDK to supported production runtime: the Agent Harness and consumption-billed Foundry Hosted Agents are now GA, shipping planning, context compaction, tool approval and OpenTelemetry on by default while gating shell, file access and auto-looping behind opt-in warnings. The piece's real argument is that the harness — not the model — is where competitive engineering now lives, backed by a VILA-Lab classification putting ~98.4% of Claude Code's codebase in harness infrastructure and a benchmark where Agent Framework self-halted at 40 round-trips while the GitHub Copilot SDK ran to 300.

themes.theme: Runtime supersedes SDK as the product

insights.claim: Microsoft has moved its Agent Framework past the SDK stage into a supported production runtime, with the Agent Harness and Foundry Hosted Agents both reaching general availability and running as a single binary across local development, containers, and hosted deployment.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: The monetizable layer in enterprise agents is shifting from build-time libraries to governed runtime hosting; watch Azure/Foundry consumption revenue rather than SDK adoption counts.
insights.quote: It runs as one binary across local development, containers, and hosted deployment.
insights.locator: Microsoft has moved Agent Framework past

insights.claim: Microsoft Agent Framework reached 1.0 general availability on April 2, 2026 as the open-source consolidation of Semantic Kernel and AutoGen, moving both predecessor frameworks to maintenance mode.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Framework fragmentation inside Microsoft's agent stack is over; teams standardizing on Semantic Kernel or AutoGen face a forced migration, which concentrates ecosystem gravity on one runtime.
insights.quote: The 1.0 release settled the build-time question of which framework to use and moved both predecessors to maintenance mode.
insights.locator: Earlier, InfoQ covered the framework's launch

insights.claim: The competitive questions in enterprise agent platforms have moved from build-time (which framework to use) to run-time: where agents execute, what they are allowed to touch, and how their behavior surfaces in existing observability and policy systems.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: A durable lens for evaluating any agent vendor: score execution locus, permission surface, and telemetry integration rather than feature lists or model quality.
insights.quote: The Build announcements address the run-time questions that follow: where agents execute, what they are allowed to touch, and how their behavior surfaces in existing observability and policy systems.
insights.locator: Earlier, InfoQ covered the framework's launch

insights.claim: Foundry Hosted Agents, Microsoft's managed deployment target for agents, bills on consumption rather than seats or licenses.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Consumption billing ties Microsoft's agent revenue directly to agent loop volume, making round-trip counts and looping defaults a revenue variable as well as a safety one.
insights.quote: Foundry Hosted Agents, the managed deployment target, bills on consumption.
insights.locator: The harness is the center of that

insights.claim: The Microsoft Agent Harness ships function invocation, per-call history persistence, context compaction, a todo list with plan and execute modes, file memory, skills, web search, tool approval, and built-in OpenTelemetry — all enabled by default and each individually removable.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: This is the commoditization checklist: startups selling context compaction, agent memory, or approval gating as standalone products now compete with a default-on feature in a Microsoft runtime.
insights.quote: each enabled by default and individually removable
insights.locator: The harness is the center of that

insights.claim: Shell tooling, file access, background sub-agents, and automatic looping are excluded from the Agent Harness defaults, remaining opt-in and emitting a warning even when a developer enables them.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Microsoft is explicitly risk-tiering agent capabilities; the four gated behaviors mark where enterprise liability and security-tooling demand will concentrate.
insights.quote: Shell tooling, file access, background sub-agents, and automatic looping remain opt-in and still emit a warning when enabled.
insights.locator: The harness is the center of that

insights.claim: A single create_harness_agent call in the Agent Framework wires in planning, history persistence, compaction, approvals, web search, and telemetry, leaving developers to supply only a chat client, instructions, and tools.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Low integration friction accelerates default adoption inside Azure shops; the switching cost accrues to whoever owns the one-call abstraction.
insights.locator: Developers supply a chat client, instructions

themes.theme: The 98.4% harness claim and its asterisks

insights.claim: An April 2026 paper from MBZUAI's VILA-Lab, "Dive into Claude Code," classified roughly 512,000 lines across 1,884 files of Claude Code v2.1.88 and estimated that about 98.4% of the codebase is harness infrastructure while only about 1.6% is AI decision logic.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: If ~98% of a leading coding agent is plumbing, agent-company valuations resting on model access are mispriced relative to those resting on runtime engineering.
insights.quote: about 98.4% of the codebase is harness infrastructure, permissions, context management, sandboxing, tool routing, and recovery, and about 1.6% is AI decision logic
insights.locator: Why a supported harness matters more than

insights.claim: The Claude Code source that enabled the VILA-Lab analysis was briefly exposed on March 31 when Anthropic shipped an npm release containing a sourcemap bundle, revealing the full TypeScript source of v2.1.88.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Competitive intelligence on closed agent runtimes can arrive via packaging accidents; supply-chain hygiene at AI vendors is itself a moat-integrity issue.
insights.quote: whose full TypeScript source was briefly exposed on March 31 when Anthropic shipped an npm release with a sourcemap bundle
insights.locator: Why a supported harness matters more than

insights.claim: The 98.4% harness figure should be discounted because it is a line-count classification of a leak-derived bundle that includes generated and minified code, not a universal audit of agent architecture.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Treat the headline number as directional, not quantitative — anyone citing 98.4% as a hard architectural constant is overreaching.
insights.quote: it is a line-count classification of a leak-derived bundle that includes generated and minified code, not a universal audit
insights.locator: Why a supported harness matters more than

insights.claim: Several independently built coding agents, including Codex CLI and Aider, converged on the same harness shape as Claude Code, implying the architecture is a constraint imposed by the problem rather than a design preference.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Convergent architecture means harness design is not a differentiator long-term; durable advantage will come from governance, hosting, and distribution instead.
insights.quote: several independently built agents, among them Codex CLI and Aider, converged on the same harness shape, suggesting a constraint of the problem rather than a design choice
insights.locator: Why a supported harness matters more than

themes.theme: Runaway-loop safety as the real differentiator

insights.claim: A head-to-head benchmark holding the model fixed found that the Agent Framework and the GitHub Copilot SDK reached identical answers in the same number of steps, with all meaningful differences located in the runtime rather than the reasoning — summarized as "same reasoning, different engineering".
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Model benchmarks are losing discriminating power for agent products; buyer evaluation is migrating to runtime behavior under stress.
insights.locator: An early benchmark points the same way

insights.claim: In that benchmark the Agent Framework halted its own loop after 40 round-trips and returned a limit-reached message, while the GitHub Copilot SDK with host-side stopping controls off ran to 300 round-trips without stopping on its own.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Where the brake lives — inside the agent loop or in the host — is the single sharpest question for cost control and runaway-spend risk on consumption-billed agent platforms.
insights.quote: One harness keeps the brake inside the loop; the other expects the host to supply it.
insights.locator: An early benchmark points the same way

insights.claim: The Agent Framework versus Copilot SDK benchmark was run by Microsoft AI principal architect Aqib Sherwani and compares two Microsoft-owned runtimes, though its method held the model fixed and ran a deterministic mock first so variance traces to the harness.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Methodologically stronger than typical vendor benchmarks but structurally conflicted; discount the framing while keeping the round-trip numbers.
insights.quote: The method is more disciplined than most vendor benchmarks, holding the model fixed and running a deterministic mock first so variance traces to the harness.
insights.locator: An early benchmark points the same way

themes.theme: Third-party coding agents as governed fleet members

insights.claim: An Agent Framework orchestration can delegate to the GitHub Copilot SDK or the Claude Agent SDK without custom adapters, wrapping each agent's own autonomous loop so it composes alongside Azure OpenAI, Anthropic, or custom agents in a single workflow.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Microsoft is positioning as the orchestration layer above rival coding agents rather than trying to displace them — a distribution play that makes Anthropic a component, not a competitor, inside Azure estates.
insights.locator: The coding-agent connectors make the governance story

insights.claim: The Agent Framework connectors force third-party coding agents to honor the identity, content safety, and observability policies already set for the fleet, landing their traffic in the same OpenTelemetry traces and Foundry dashboards instead of creating a separate integration with its own access model.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Policy unification is the enterprise wedge; vendors whose agents cannot be governed through an existing control plane will be blocked at procurement.
insights.quote: Coding-agent traffic lands in the same OpenTelemetry traces and Foundry dashboards as everything else, rather than becoming a separate integration with its own access model.
insights.locator: The coding-agent connectors make the governance story

insights.claim: The governing question for agent platforms is shifting from what an agent can do to who ran it, under which policy, and where the trace lands — a control-layer concern also visible in AWS's Loom reference platform.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Both hyperscalers are converging on agent governance as the battleground; identity, audit, and telemetry vendors sit directly in that path.
insights.quote: the governing question shifts from what an agent can do to who ran it, under which policy, and where the trace lands
insights.locator: The coding-agent connectors make the governance story

themes.theme: Orchestration patterns and the Magentic evidence base

insights.claim: The Agent Framework's orchestration patterns — sequential pipelines, parallel collaboration, and the Magentic pattern — reached stable release sharing one API, so teams can change coordination styles without rewriting agent code.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: A shared coordination API lowers the cost of experimenting with multi-agent topologies, which should accelerate real multi-agent deployment beyond pilots.
insights.quote: The patterns share one API, so teams change coordination styles without rewriting agent code.
insights.locator: The orchestration patterns reached stable release

insights.claim: The Magentic pattern derives from Microsoft Research's Magentic-One, whose 2024 evaluation reported 38% on GAIA, 27.7% on AssistantBench, and 32.8% on WebArena, with Microsoft self-reporting the WebArena figure because that benchmark has no hidden test set.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: The stable orchestration pattern rests on two-year-old benchmark numbers, one of them self-reported — evidence for multi-agent efficacy remains thinner than the GA label implies.
insights.quote: which Microsoft reported itself because the benchmark has no hidden test set
insights.locator: The orchestration patterns reached stable release
